column2: The state of being an individual soul is not different from that (Self), for the Self is by nature distinct from it; the connection of the Self with the intellect is preceded by false knowledge.
The cessation of that connection of the Self comes only through right knowledge, not otherwise. The knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self is right knowledge, according to scripture.
That is accomplished only by right discrimination between the Self and the not-Self; therefore discrimination is to be practised between the inner Self and the unreal self.
As water, very muddy, becomes clear when the mud is removed, though it appeared as if unclear like the mud, so the Self too, when its impurity is absent, shines clearly.
When the unreal is removed, the recognition of this inner Self as the real Self becomes clear; therefore the rejection of the "I" and the like, the unreal self, is certainly to be done.

Therefore this (knowledge-sheath) cannot be the Supreme Self, though called "knowledge-made": because it changes, is inert, is limited, is an object, is inconstant — what is not eternal cannot be held eternal.

The mental state, touched by the reflection of bliss and swollen with tamas, is the bliss-made (sheath), with qualities like fondness, arising on the gain of a desired object; it shines in the experience of merit for the virtuous, as bliss itself, in which every embodied being rejoices without effort.
The bliss-sheath has its strongest manifestation in deep sleep; in dream and waking it is faint, through the sight of a desired object and the like.
This bliss-made (sheath) is not the Supreme Self, because it has an adjunct, is a modification of Nature, is an effect, results from good deeds, and consists of an aggregate of modifications.
When all five sheaths have been denied, by reasoning and by scripture, what remains at the end of the denial is the witness, of the nature of awareness.
This Self — self-luminous, distinct from the five sheaths, the witness of the three states, unchanging and stainless, ever blissful — is to be known by the wise as his own Self.

The disciple said: "Master, when these five sheaths have been denied as unreal, I see nothing here but the absence of everything. What real thing is there left to be known by the wise one through the Self?"
The revered teacher said: "You say truly, wise one; you are skilled in reasoning. The modifications beginning with 'I' are yours (to be denied), and their absence too, is known likewise."
That by which all these are experienced, and which is itself not experienced — know that Self, the knower, with a very subtle mind.
Whatever is experienced by anything has that (experiencer) as its witness; where a thing is not experienced by anyone, there is no use for a witness.
This state of being one's own witness is not possible for anything else, since it is experienced by itself; therefore the supreme is directly the inner Self, and nothing else.

That which shines forth so clearly in waking, dream and deep sleep, as the inner Self, ever flashing within as 'I, I' in many ways, seeing all these modifications of various forms, headed by the sense of 'I', and shining as eternal bliss and consciousness — know this as your own in the heart.
Seeing the disc of the sun reflected in the water of a pot, the fool takes it for the sun itself; so the dull one, through delusion, takes the reflected consciousness abiding in the adjunct as 'I'.
Leaving aside the pot, the water and the sun's image in it, one looks at the sun in the sky, which, standing apart, illumines these three; so, for the wise, the Self is self-luminous.

Thus, having set aside the body, the intellect and the reflection of consciousness, and finding the Self that dwells in the cave of the intellect — the seer, of undivided knowledge, the light of all, distinct from being and non-being —
eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, very subtle, empty of inside and outside, non-different from oneself — a man who has rightly known this own form of himself,

becomes free from sin, stain and death, free from sorrow, a mass of bliss, a knower; he fears nothing from anything. There is no other way for the seeker of liberation from the bonds of worldly existence than knowing his own truth.
The knowledge of one's non-difference from Brahman is the cause of release from worldly existence, by which the wise attain Brahman, the non-dual bliss.
One who has become Brahman does not return to worldly existence; therefore the non-difference of the Self from Brahman must be rightly known.
Brahman — truth, knowledge, infinite, pure, supreme, self-established, of one taste of eternal bliss, non-different from the inner Self, unbroken — is victorious.
This is the supreme non-duality, since there is nothing else apart from itself. Nothing else at all exists, in the state of right knowledge of the ultimate truth.
This whole universe, appearing in many forms through ignorance — all that is only Brahman, when the fault of every false imagination has been cast away.
A pot, though an effect of clay, is not different from clay; everywhere it is only the nature of clay. The form of a pot exists nowhere apart; so how is a pot anything but a name falsely imagined?
No one can show the pot as something different from clay; therefore the pot is only imagined through delusion — clay alone is true, the ultimate reality.
Thus the whole effect of Brahman is the Real alone; it is only that, nothing else. He who says 'it is not' — his delusion is not gone; he babbles like one asleep.

'All this universe is Brahman' — so speaks the excellent voice of scripture, rooted in the Atharva Veda. Therefore this universe is Brahman alone; what is superimposed is not different from its substratum.
If the universe were real, the infinity of the Self would be lost, the Vedas would lose authority, and the Lord would be guilty of falsehood — none of these three is acceptable to the great.
'The Lord, who knows the truth of things, says: I do not abide in them, and beings do not abide in me' — thus (He) declared.
If the universe were real, let it be perceived in deep sleep; since nothing is perceived there, it is unreal, false like a dream.

Therefore the world is not separate from the Supreme Self; its being perceived as separate is false, like a quality of the rope-snake. What reality has the superimposed? The substratum shines thus through delusion.
Whatever is perceived by a deluded man through delusion is only Brahman, as the silver is the shell; Brahman is always taken as 'this,' while what is superimposed on Brahman is a mere name.
Beyond this is Brahman, real, non-dual, a mass of pure knowledge, stainless, tranquil, without beginning or end, actionless, of the nature of the taste of unbroken bliss —
free of all the differences made by Maya, eternal happiness, without parts, immeasurable, eternal, steady, formless, unmanifest, nameless, imperishable, self-luminous — shining as something.
Devoid of knower, known and knowledge, infinite, free of alternatives, mere undivided consciousness — this the wise know as the supreme truth.
Not to be rejected, not to be taken up, beyond the reach of mind and speech, immeasurable, without beginning or end — Brahman, the full, great light, am I.

When the meanings of the words "that" and "thou" are thus purified, Brahman and the Self, the scripture, by "That thou art," repeatedly teaches their oneness rightly. Their oneness is expressed through the implied, not the literal, meanings of the two whose apparent attributes are contradictory — like a firefly and the sun, a king and his servant, a well and the ocean, an atom and Mount Meru.

This contradiction between them is imagined through the adjunct, not real; it is just the adjunct. The Lord's adjunct is Maya, the cause beginning with the Great Principle; the soul's is the effect — hear: the five sheaths.

When these two adjuncts of the Supreme and the soul are entirely removed, there is neither Supreme nor soul — as, when the king's kingdom and the soldier's shield are taken away, there is neither soldier nor king.
Now therefore the teaching — the scripture itself denies the duality imagined in Brahman. By the knowledge upheld by the authority of scripture, the removal of the two must be accomplished.

Not this, not this — because it is imagined it is not real, like a snake seen in a rope, or like a dream. Having removed what is seen, by sound reasoning, the identity of the two (Brahman and the Self) is to be known afterward.

Then the two, well indicated by implication, are to be understood in their undivided oneness; neither the giving-up implication nor the not-giving-up implication suffices; it must be a combination of both.

As in "This is that Devadatta," oneness is stated by setting aside the parts with contradictory attributes, so in the sentence "That thou art" one should set aside the contradictory attributes on both sides.

Having recognised, by pure consciousness alone, the real Self in both, the wise know the undivided state. Thus, by hundreds of great sayings, the oneness of Brahman and the Self, the undivided state, is taught.

Having rejected the unreal by "not gross" and the like, the Self is established by itself, unthinkable like space. Therefore give up this appearing, merely false thing which you have taken as your self. By pure understanding know your own Self as "I am Brahman," of undivided knowledge.

As all effects of clay, such as pots, are always only clay, so all this, born of the Real, is only the Real; since there is nothing whatever beyond the Real, that Real is the Self itself; therefore you are That — the tranquil, stainless Brahman, non-dual, the supreme.

As all that belongs to a dream — place, time, objects, knower and the rest — is false, so in waking too the world is an effect of one's own ignorance. Since thus this body, organs, breath and ego are unreal, therefore you are That — the tranquil, stainless Brahman, non-dual, the supreme.

What is imagined through delusion is, on discrimination, only that (substratum) and not different from it. The manifold dream-universe vanished in dream — is it seen as different from oneself on waking?
Beyond caste, rule, family and lineage, free of name, form, quality and fault, transcending place, time and object — that Brahman you are; meditate on it in the Self.

That supreme, beyond the reach of all speech, yet within the range of the eye of pure knowledge; the pure, dense consciousness, the beginningless reality — that Brahman you are; meditate on it in the Self.
Free from the six waves; contemplated in the hearts of yogis and not by the senses; not known by the intellect, blameless — that Brahman you are; meditate on it in the Self.

The support of the parts of the universe imagined through delusion, its own support, distinct from being and non-being, without parts, without comparison — that Brahman you are; meditate on it in the Self.

Devoid of birth, growth, transformation, decay, disease and death, imperishable, the cause of the creation, maintenance and dissolution of the universe — that Brahman you are; meditate on it in the Self.
Free of differences, its characteristics undenied, motionless like a waveless ocean, ever free, of undivided form — that Brahman you are; meditate on it in the Self.
One alone, the real, the cause of the many, the cause that removes any other cause, itself without cause, distinct from cause and effect — that Brahman you are; meditate on it in the Self.
Free of alternatives, great, imperishable, distinct from the perishable and the imperishable, supreme, of eternal, unchanging happiness, stainless — that Brahman you are; meditate on it in the Self.
That which, through delusion, shines as manifold through name, form, quality and change, yet itself is always unchanged like gold — that Brahman you are; meditate on it in the Self.

That which shines with nothing beyond it, beyond the beyond, the inner one, of one taste, having the Self as its mark, being-consciousness-bliss, infinite, imperishable — that Brahman you are; meditate on it in the Self.

Let one contemplate in oneself, with the mind, by well-known reasonings, this matter that has been stated; being free of doubts, like water in the palm, thus the truth of the scriptures will be known.
Having known the pure truth, mere awareness, as a king (is known) among an army, taking refuge in that and always abiding in the Self, dissolve the whole produced world in Brahman.
Brahman exists — real, supreme, non-dual, distinct from being and non-being, in the cave of the intellect. He who here abides in that cave as that (Brahman) has no more entry into the cave of a womb.

Even when the Reality is known, this beginningless habit-impression, "I am the doer and enjoyer," which is strong, is the cause of worldly existence for him; it must be removed with effort by dwelling in the Self with inward vision. This the sages call liberation: the thinning out of habit-impressions.
The feeling "I" and "mine" in the not-Self — body, senses and the like — is this superimposition; it is to be discarded by the wise through steadfastness in the Self.
Having known your own inner Self, the witness of the intellect and its functions, with the right thought "That am I," give up the idea of self in the not-Self.
Giving up following the world, giving up following the body, giving up following the scriptures (as ends), remove the superimposition on yourself.

Through the habit-impressions of the world, of the scriptures and of the body, knowledge does not arise in a creature as it should. The knowers say that a strong triple habit-impression is the iron chain fettering the feet of one who wishes release from the prison of worldly existence; he who is freed from it attains liberation.
Like the divine fragrance of aloe-wood, covered by the foul smell arising from contact with water and the like, shines clearly by rubbing when the outer smell is washed away —
so the fragrance of the Supreme Self, smeared with the dust of endless, endless habit-impressions lying within, appears clearly, purified by the rubbing of wisdom, like the scent of sandalwood.
The fragrance of the Self, hidden by the net of habit-impressions of the not-Self, shines clear of itself when they are destroyed by steadfastness in the eternal Self.
As the mind abides more and more in the inner Self, so it lets go of external habit-impressions; when they are completely removed, the experience of the Self becomes free of obstruction.
By always abiding in the Self, the yogi's mind is destroyed; so, through that abiding, the habit-impressions are exhausted; therefore remove the superimposition on yourself.
Tamas is destroyed by the two (rajas and sattva); rajas by sattva; and sattva by the pure; therefore, relying on sattva, remove the superimposition on yourself.
Knowing that the body is sustained by prarabdha karma, being unshaken, taking up courage, remove the superimposition on yourself with effort.
I am not the individual but the Supreme Brahman — with this negation of what is other, remove the superimposition on yourself that has come through the force of habit-impressions.
Having known by scripture, reasoning and your own experience that the Self is the Self of all, remove the superimposition on yourself that occasionally appears.
For the sage there is hardly any action of taking or giving up; therefore, by steadfastness in that alone, always remove the superimposition on yourself.
Through the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self arising from sentences such as "That thou art," for firmness of the notion of Self in Brahman, remove the superimposition on yourself.
Until the sense of "I" in this body is completely dissolved, with attentive and concentrated mind, remove the superimposition on yourself.
As long as the appearance of the individual and the world shines like a dream, so long, O wise one, incessantly remove the superimposition on yourself.
Giving no opening to sleep, to worldly talk, to sound and the like, or to forgetfulness, contemplate the Self in the Self.
Casting far away, like an outcaste, this body born of the impurity of mother and father, made of filth and flesh, become Brahman and be one who has done his duty.
Merging the Self in the Supreme Self, as the space in a pot in the great space, in undivided being, be always silent, O sage.
Being silent, having become by yourself the self-luminous substratum, in the real Self, let the cosmic egg and the body-egg be abandoned like a pot of filth.
Fixing the "I"-notion that has climbed on the body upon the Self of consciousness, ever-blissful, and casting off the subtle body, be forever alone.
That in which this appearance of the world shines like a city in a mirror — knowing "That Brahman am I," you will have fulfilled your task.
Having reached that real, primal nature of oneself — consciousness, non-dual bliss, formless, actionless — let him cast off the false body, like an actor the costume he has put on.
All this visible world is utterly false; "I" is not its object, since it is seen to be momentary. How could the notion "I know everything" be established for the momentary ego and the rest?

The meaning of "I" is the witness of the ego and the rest, existing constantly, even in deep sleep, as is seen; scripture itself says "unborn, eternal" — that inner Self is distinct from being and non-being.
The knower of all modifications of the changing can be eternal and unchanging; the non-existence of both those (changing things) is seen clearly again and again in day-dreams, dreams and deep sleep.
Therefore give up self-conceit in this lump of flesh, and also in the ego imagined by the intellect; having known your own Self, undivided knowledge, unobstructed in the three times, attain peace.

Give up pride in family, lineage, name, form and stages of life, which belong to the wet corpse (the body); having also given up the properties of the subtle body, such as agency, become of the nature of undivided bliss.
There are other obstacles seen for a person which cause worldly existence; the root of them all is the first modification, egoism.
As long as there is any connection of oneself with this evil egoism, so long not even a hint of the talk of liberation is possible.
Freed from the seizure by the crocodile of egoism, one attains one's own nature — stainless like the moon, full, ever-blissful, self-luminous.
That which in the body is perceived as "I," made up by the intellect, deluded by tamas — when that is destroyed entirely, the state of Brahman and the Self, free of all obstacles, is reached.

The treasure of the bliss of Brahman is guarded, coiled around by the terrible serpent of egoism, mighty, with three fierce heads made of the qualities; having cut off the three heads with the great sword called knowledge, taught by scripture, and uprooted this serpent, the steadfast man is able to enjoy the treasure that brings happiness.
